catalog_quote: Although the convention does not use any tone mark, we shall put ´, ˆ, and ˇ on the vowel with high tone, falling tone, and rising tone,1) respectively. A vowel without any tone mark on it is low-toned. The homorganic nasal after a vowel with ´, ˆ, or ˇ is pronounced high, low, or high, and the vowel itself is pronounced high, high, or low, respectively. Generally speaking, ˆ and ˇ appear only on the penultimate syllable af a word before a pause, but we will find some exceptions in sections to follow. When the penultimate syllable is low and the final syllable is high, the latter is usually pronounced with falling tone when it is followed by a pause, but, as there seems to be no contrast of high vs. falling for the final syllable, we shall represent it by ´. ... In the tonal representation employed in this paper, a consonant or a consonant plus a semivowel, a vowel (there seems to be no long vowel in this language), or a homorganic nasal is represented by the third reader, V, or N, respectively.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nkoya is described purely as a tone language: syllables are high or low, with falling and rising contour tones that (with stated exceptions) occur only on the penultimate syllable of a pre-pausal word; there are no long vowels. Verb tone is lexical (two verb classes A/B) and grammatical (subject-prefix and object-prefix classes, tense forms). The source makes no statement at all about word stress or accentual prominence; no claim that a stress exists or is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tonal exceptions: contour tones outside the pre-pausal penult in some verb forms; 'delayed falling' on the syllable after a high; final H realized as falling before pause. Nothing stress-related.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements are about the word before a pause (citation/pre-pausal forms) versus forms followed by other material; the study covers verb forms elicited from one speaker (Lusaka, 1985-6, informant from Shumina village near Lalafuta/Kaoma).
new_statements.identity_note: Yukawa's data are from one speaker (Mwiitila Chrispin, b. 1960, Shumina village near Lalafuta, not far from Kaoma), i.e. Nkoya proper of the Kaoma area (nkoy1244); Wikipedia/Maho treat Mbwera, Kolwe, Shangi, Shasha as distinct varieties of an Nkoya cluster, none of which this source covers.

tone_statements.citation: Yukawa, Yasutoshi (1987). A tonal study of Nkoya verbs. In Studies in Zambian languages. Tokyo: Institute for the Study of Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo Universit. pp. 129-184.
tone_statements.quote: この言語の動詞は,それ自体としてアクセントの面から2つの型に分けられる。不定形(構造:ku+語幹+a)で見ると,kǔla,「食べる」,kumôna「見る」,kumónesha「見せる」といったもの(A型)と,kuwisha「倒す」,kulongesha「教える」といったもの(B型)とである。対格接辞が語幹直前にはいることがあり,その如何によってアクセントの差が生まれる。...直説法各形では,主格接辞の如何によってもアクセントに差が出ることが多い。
tone_statements.translation: The verbs of this language divide, in themselves, into two types with respect to accent. Seen in the infinitive (structure: ku+stem+a), they are ones like kǔla 'eat', kumôna 'see', kumónesha 'show' (type A) and ones like kuwisha 'knock down', kulongesha 'teach' (type B). An object prefix may come immediately before the stem, and depending on it a difference of accent arises. ... In the indicative forms, differences of accent also often appear depending on the subject prefix.
tone_statements.locator: p. 124, paragraphs 2-3 of the Yukawa summary
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Conference summary: Nkoya verbs form two accent (tone) types A/B; tone shifts with object/subject prefixes. Examples bear acute, circumflex, caron marks; no inventory or count; nothing on stress.

sources.note: Nothing about stress. Introduction (pp. 129-130) gives the orthography and a tone system of high, low, falling and rising tones; falling/rising tones are said to occur only on the penultimate syllable of a word before a pause; no long vowels. The whole chapter is a verb-tone study (56 pp.); a full-text search for stress/accent full scanned for stress/accent/prominence/lengthening finds nothing.

sources.note: Survey of Bantu tone by the same author; p. 37 uses Nkoya future-tense verb forms (ni-ka-mónesh-a etc.) to illustrate a language that preserves all three tonal oppositions (subject prefix class, object prefix class, verb-stem class). Treats Nkoya as a tone ('accent') language; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: 湯川恭敏 (Yukawa, Yasutoshi). 1986 [printed 1987]. ンコヤ語動詞アクセント試論 [A tentative tonal analysis of Nkoya verbs]. アジア・アフリカ文法研究 15 (Asian and African Linguistics 15: 1986), 1-51. Tokyo: ILCAA. ISBN 4-87297-302-X.
sources.note: Japanese original of the 1987 English chapter (so stated on p. 182 of the English version). Uses アクセント for pitch: marks high, falling and rising vowels against unmarked low; falling/rising only on the pre-pausal penult; no long vowels. No mention of 強勢/stress in the pages scanned (pp. 1-4).
